commands.desc: Rebase while keeping stacked branches updated
commands.tooltip: During an interactive rebase, --update-refs also moves any branch that points at a rebased commit, so stacked branches follow their base. Without it those branches keep pointing at the old commits. It only affects local branches.

commands.desc: Rebase while preserving merge commits
commands.tooltip: Interactive rebase normally flattens merges away; --rebase-merges keeps the merge structure and re-creates the merge commits on the new base. It is essential for rebasing branches with intentional merge topology. Conflicts may need to be re-resolved at each merge.

commands.desc: Run a command after every rebased commit
commands.tooltip: Runs the given command after each commit is replayed, stopping the rebase if it fails. Use it to verify every step still passes tests during a long rebase. The -x shorthand works the same.

commands.desc: Rewrite history back to the first commit
commands.tooltip: Extends an interactive rebase to the very first commit instead of stopping at a fixed HEAD~N. Useful for fixing the root commit or its author. Rewriting the root changes every commit hash, so never do it on published history.

commands.desc: Undo a bad reset using the reflog
commands.tooltip: Resets to the state recorded one step ago in the reflog, the standard escape hatch after a destructive reset --hard. The reflog logs every HEAD movement, so the lost commit is usually still reachable. Do this before garbage collection prunes the orphaned objects.

commands.desc: Reset your branch to match the remote
commands.tooltip: Throws away all local commits and working-tree changes on the current branch, pointing it at origin/main exactly. Every local-only commit is lost, so check git log first. Prefer it only when the local branch is known to be garbage.

commands.desc: Reset while preserving local changes
commands.tooltip: Moves the branch back one commit but keeps working-tree and staged changes intact, aborting if they conflict with the reset. It is a safer middle ground between --mixed and --hard. Files touched only by the reset get updated.

commands.desc: Reset without losing overlapping changes
commands.tooltip: Resets to the given commit but refuses if the working tree has changes that overlap with the difference. It can also cancel an in-progress merge cleanly. When it fails, stash or commit before resetting.

commands.desc: Inspect the reflog five steps back
commands.tooltip: Shows the state of HEAD five moves ago, complete with the hash and what changed. Combined with git reset --hard HEAD@{5} it restores exactly that point. The reflog is local to your machine and expires after 90 days by default.

commands.desc: Revert a commit without committing yet
commands.tooltip: Computes the inverse of the named commit and stages it in the index and working tree, leaving the revert commit for you to make. Combine several -n reverts into one commit, or review before committing. It is the batch-friendly revert.

commands.desc: Revert a merge commit
commands.tooltip: Undoes a merge by replaying its inverse against one of its parents; -m 1 selects the first parent, usually the mainline. Reverting a merge without -m fails because the direction is ambiguous. The reverted change still exists in the merged branch's history.

commands.desc: Finish a revert after resolving conflicts
commands.tooltip: Completes a conflicted revert once the files are fixed and staged, reusing the prepared revert message. It is the revert counterpart of git rebase --continue. Resolve and git add every conflicted file first.

commands.desc: Cancel an in-progress revert
commands.tooltip: Stops the current revert and restores the branch and working tree to their pre-revert state. All conflict resolutions made during the attempt are discarded. It is the clean escape when a revert gets messy.

commands.desc: Cherry-pick and record the source commit
commands.tooltip: Applies the named commit to the current branch and appends a line noting the original commit hash in the new message. The -x trailer makes provenance traceable across branches. Use it when cherry-picking between long-lived branches.

commands.desc: Cherry-pick without committing
commands.tooltip: Applies the changes from the named commit to the index and working tree without creating a commit. It is useful for staging several picks and committing them as one. The -n shorthand stands for --no-commit.

commands.desc: Finish a cherry-pick after fixing conflicts
commands.tooltip: Completes a conflicted cherry-pick once conflicts are resolved and staged, keeping the original commit message. It is the cherry-pick counterpart of git rebase --continue. Resolve all conflicts and git add the files first.

commands.desc: Cancel an in-progress cherry-pick
commands.tooltip: Stops the current cherry-pick and restores the branch to its state before the operation began. Any conflict resolutions made along the way are discarded. Run it when a pick turns out to be more trouble than it is worth.

commands.desc: Create a GPG-signed commit
commands.tooltip: Signs the commit with your GPG key so others can verify its authorship. Configure the key with git config user.signingkey and enable signing by default with commit.gpgsign true. Verify signatures with git verify-commit.

commands.desc: Rewrite the last commit with your identity
commands.tooltip: Amends the most recent commit and resets its author to your configured identity, fixing commits made with the wrong name or email. Handy after realizing you committed with a work account. Amending changes the hash, so avoid it on pushed commits.

commands.desc: Verify a commit's GPG signature
commands.tooltip: Checks the GPG signature on the named commit against the signer's key and reports whether it is valid. Commits that are not signed produce an error, which scripts can use as a gate. The -v flag prints the full commit contents alongside.

commands.desc: Skip an unbuildable commit during bisect
commands.tooltip: Marks the current commit as un-testable and moves the search to another candidate, since a broken build would pollute the results. Use it when a commit cannot compile or the test cannot run. The search continues between the remaining good and bad boundaries.

commands.desc: Show the current bisect progress
commands.tooltip: Prints the entire bisect session: the start points and every good, bad, and skip marking so far. It lets you verify the session or replay it later with git bisect replay. Run it before git bisect reset to keep a record.

commands.desc: Remove stale worktree bookkeeping
commands.tooltip: Cleans up administrative data for worktrees whose directories were deleted behind Git's back. Git normally prunes automatically, but crashes and manual deletions leave clutter. Run git worktree list to see what remains.

commands.desc: Compare two versions of a branch
commands.tooltip: Shows how two commit ranges relate commit by commit, pairing equivalent patches and marking changed, added, or dropped ones. It is the standard tool for reviewing a rebase or a cherry-pick batch. The symmetric-difference syntax a...b is the common form.

commands.desc: Generate a patch file for the last commit
commands.tooltip: Writes the latest commit as an email-style patch file named 0001-subject.patch in the current directory. Others can apply it with git am. The -1 limits it to one commit; use -3 or a range for more.

commands.desc: Stream a patch series and apply it
commands.tooltip: The left side prints the last three commits as one patch stream; the right side applies them with three-way merging where needed. The -3 on am falls back to a three-way merge against the original blobs when a patch does not apply cleanly. This is the classic email-based contribution pipeline.

commands.desc: Package the repo into a single file
commands.tooltip: Writes the entire repository, including all branches and tags, into one portable bundle file. Transfer the file to another machine and clone or fetch from it without any network. It is the standard offline transfer and backup format.

commands.desc: Check a bundle's integrity
commands.tooltip: Validates that the bundle file is well-formed, its prerequisites are satisfied, and its commits are reachable. Run it before cloning from a bundle you received. It reports which prerequisite commits are missing.

commands.desc: List the refs inside a bundle
commands.tooltip: Shows every branch and tag contained in the bundle file without unpacking it. It is the inspection step before deciding which ref to clone or fetch. The heads are the entry points into the bundled history.

commands.desc: Strip a file from all of history
commands.tooltip: Removes the named path from every commit, rewriting all affected hashes, so the file is gone from the entire history. filter-repo is the maintained successor to filter-branch, which the Git project now recommends against. Anyone with a clone of the old history can still retrieve the file, so rotate any exposed secrets.

commands.desc: Profile repository history for cleanup
commands.tooltip: Scans the whole history and writes a report of the largest files, biggest extensions, and busiest paths into .git/filter-repo/. It is the first step before rewriting history with --strip-blobs-bigger-than or --path. The analysis itself changes nothing.

commands.desc: Enable sparse checkout with cone mode
commands.tooltip: Turns on sparse checkout, so future checkouts only materialize the directories you choose. Cone mode is the simpler, recommended pattern matching. Follow with git sparse-checkout set to pick directories.

commands.desc: Limit the working tree to one directory
commands.tooltip: Restricts the checkout to the given directory, shrinking disk use in huge monorepos. Files outside the set are removed from the working tree but stay in the repository. Add more directories with git sparse-checkout add.

commands.desc: Restore a full checkout
commands.tooltip: Turns sparse checkout off and materializes the entire working tree again. It is the undo for a limited checkout. The repository data was never missing, only the on-disk files.

commands.desc: Set up Git LFS for this machine
commands.tooltip: Registers Git LFS hooks and filters so large files tracked with LFS are handled transparently. Git LFS stores big files outside the repository and swaps in small pointer files. Run it once per machine after installing git-lfs.

commands.desc: Tell Git LFS to manage a file type
commands.tooltip: Adds a pattern to .gitattributes so matching files, here Photoshop files, are stored as LFS pointers instead of blobs. The pointer keeps the commit small while the real content lives on the LFS server. Commit the .gitattributes change.

commands.desc: List files stored in Git LFS
commands.tooltip: Shows every file the repository tracks with LFS, including its size and the commit that added it. Use it to audit how much data LFS is carrying. Add --long for full hashes and --all to include every revision.

commands.desc: Convert existing files to Git LFS
commands.tooltip: Rewrites history so matching files are stored as LFS pointers retroactively, shrinking the repository. It rewrites every affected commit hash and requires a force push, so coordinate with the whole team first. Back up the repository before running it.

commands.desc: Find objects not reachable from any ref
commands.tooltip: Lists commits, trees, and blobs that no branch, tag, or reflog reaches, often the remains of rebases and resets. These are candidates for recovery with git show or for pruning with git gc. The --lost-found option writes dangling objects to disk.

commands.desc: Force garbage collection immediately
commands.tooltip: Runs a full garbage collection and prunes unreferenced objects right away instead of respecting the default grace period. Any commit only reachable via the reflog or dangling objects is permanently deleted. Only run it after you are certain nothing needs recovery.

commands.desc: Resolve conflicts in favor of the incoming branch
commands.tooltip: The -X theirs strategy option makes merge conflicts resolve automatically to the incoming branch's version, while -X ours prefers the current branch. It removes the manual conflict step but can silently drop the losing side's changes. Reserve it for well-understood merges.

commands.desc: Push every ref to mirror a remote
commands.tooltip: Pushes all branches, tags, and remote-tracking refs, and deletes anything on the remote that is missing locally, making it an exact copy. It can destroy branches on the remote, so never point it at a shared repository. It is meant for backup and migration mirrors.

commands.desc: Search every commit for a pattern
commands.tooltip: Expands git rev-list --all into every commit hash and greps each one's tree, turning git grep into a whole-history search. It is how you hunt for secrets or deleted code across all time. Expect slow runs on large repositories.

commands.desc: Ignore local changes to a tracked file
commands.tooltip: Marks the file so Git ignores local modifications to it, keeping the committed version intact. It is designed for files that differ per machine, like local config, and is stronger than assume-unchanged. Revert with --no-skip-worktree when you want changes tracked again.

commands.desc: Stop ignoring local changes to a file
commands.tooltip: Clears the skip-worktree bit set earlier, so the file's local modifications are tracked and visible again in git status. It is the undo for --skip-worktree. Run it before editing the file if you want the change committed.

commands.desc: Find the common ancestor of two branches
commands.tooltip: Prints the merge base, the most recent commit shared by both branches. It is the reference point for diffs and rebases between them. Scripts use it to compute what each branch added.

commands.desc: Take your version of a conflicted file
commands.tooltip: Resolves the conflict in the named file by taking your side, stage two, of the merge. --theirs picks the incoming side instead. The file is then staged as resolved. Use it when one side is known to be correct.

commands.desc: Take the incoming version of a conflicted file
commands.tooltip: Resolves the conflict by keeping the branch being merged in, stage three, and discarding your local changes to that file. --ours is the opposite. After running it the file still needs a final commit to finish the merge.

commands.desc: Mark a commit to be amended into another
commands.tooltip: The amend: form of --fixup marks the new commit to be folded into the target using the combined message, which rebase --autosquash applies automatically. Plain --fixup discards the fixup message in favor of the target's. Both keep history tidy without manual todo editing.
